reception.text: The Olympic Peninsula Development League and the Seattle Commercial Club wanted the mountains opened to prospectors.
The Seattle Daily Times ran an editorial headlined "Conservation, and Olympic Copper."
At the American Mining Congress, F. H. Stanard attacked Pinchot and Roosevelt for making "a Siberian wilderness of the West."
No contemporary critic argued that the monument broke the Antiquities Act's smallest-area limit; the proclamation never mentioned that standard.

political_impact.text: Because it lay inside Olympic National Forest, the monument was run by the Forest Service rather than Interior.
Taft removed 160 acres to relieve a homesteader, leaving 608,480 acres.
political_impact.source: Proc. 1191, 37 Stat. 1737; Interior, General Information Regarding the National Monuments (1917), p. 59

legacy.text: Wilson's 1915 proclamation removed 309,110 acres, a little over half the monument, without stating a reason; the record points to timber and, secondarily, copper.
legacy.source: Proc. 1293, 39 Stat. 1726; Interior, General Information (1917), p. 59

legacy.text: In 1917 the Interior Department estimated the elk of the Olympic region at probably double the roughly 2,000 of 1905, crediting state laws that barred killing them.
legacy.source: Interior, General Information Regarding the National Monuments (1917), p. 58

legacy.text: Historian Hal Rothman called the monument "Roosevelt's going-away present to himself."
The monuments moved from the Forest Service to the National Park Service; Interior Secretary Ickes refused the Forest Service's request to reverse it.
Congress abolished the monument and created Olympic National Park, about 624,000 acres by Interior's estimate, returning other former monument lands to the national forest.
legacy.source: Act of June 29, 1938, ch. 812, 52 Stat. 1241; Annual Report of the Secretary of the Interior, FY1938, p. 27

legacy.text: Olympic National Park became an International Biosphere Reserve in 1976 and a World Heritage Site in 1981.

today.name: Olympic National Park
today.note: Created in 1938 in place of the abolished monument; 922,650 acres today, home to the largest fully wild herd of Roosevelt elk in the Pacific Northwest.
today.source: Act of June 29, 1938, 52 Stat. 1241; National Park Service

today.name: Olympic National Forest
today.note: Former monument lands eliminated in 1915 or left outside the 1938 park went back to the national forest.

later_actions.text: Proclamation 1862 removed 640 acres, excluding a homestead at Goblin's Gate on the Elwha.
Executive Order 6166 transferred the national monuments to the National Park Service.
Congress abolished the monument and established Olympic National Park.
Proclamation 2380 added 187,411 acres to the park.
Proclamation 2587 added 20,600 acres in the Morse Creek country.
Proclamation 3003 added 47,753 acres, including the Coastal Strip and the Queets Corridor.

uncertain: The park's size at its 1938 establishment is known only as the Interior Department's estimate of about 624,000 acres.
